podcast.title: Alanis Morissette - Wattouche Studio Encounter
podcast.body: During the recording of "Wattouche" at Tattoo Music, Alanis Morissette was present in the kitchen, as she was friends with the studio owners, Tim and Tom Thorney, and was working with them. At the time, she was a superstar, having sold 40 million records. She listened to their music, offered advice, and even made them spaghetti. "When we were making Wattouche, we walk in and I remember I was going to go get a cup of tea and a lanness more set was standing in this kitchen. ... And then she ended up coming in and like listening to our tunes and hanging out and was so cool and gave us good advice and... Made us spaghetti."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Band Name - Pezz (Origin and Spelling)
podcast.body: The band settled on the name "Pezz" because Ben Kowalewicz had many Pez dispensers in his room, which served as a band meeting spot. They added "X-RZ" to avoid potential legal issues with the Pez candy company. "And I think we settled on Pes because in my room I had a bunch of Pes dispensers all the time. We'd always have like band meetings up there. And it was just like, we couldn't think of a name. So we're like, why don't you just call it Pes and add an X-RZ so we don't get sued."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Band Name - The Other One
podcast.body: The band's initial name was "The Other One" for a handful of shows, as they struggled to decide on a permanent name. "Well, originally it was the other one. Yeah. Because we couldn't figure out a name. Yeah. So for a handful of shows who were the other one."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Band Name - Zigzag
podcast.body: After "The Other One," the band briefly used the name "Zigzag" for a single show. "And then Zigzag. That was for one show."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Band Name Challenge - Pez vs. Pezz
podcast.body: In 1996, Pezz received an email from a representative of another punk band called "Pes" on BIO Records in the United States. This band's records were available in Canadian stores, leading to a request for Pezz to change their name. They continued to use the name "Pezz" until 1999 as they didn't have a record deal at the time. "And technically, yeah, we ended up getting an email when email first came about in 1996. I got an email from a guy representing a band called Pes on BIO records in the United States. And he just basically said we have records in Canadian stores so you have to change your name."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Demoluca - Rarity and Copies
podcast.body: Their first 4-song demo, "Demoluca," released in 1994, is very rare as only 100 copies were originally made. "Demoluca, yes. Does it exist anywhere? Yeah. It's hard to find. It's hard to find. Yeah, yeah. There was only a hundred copies made."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Early Management Support
podcast.body: In their early days, Pezz operated without official management, relying on temporary managers like Susan Jazzvak and Andrew Lownsbury, who volunteered their time to help the band. "No management. Nothing. Yeah, it was a handful of like temporary managers at the time. That helped us out. Like Susan Jazzvak, Andrew, Lownsbury. Yeah. Yeah, just people that would donate their time, literally, to help us."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Early Toronto Music Scene Networking
podcast.body: After gaining a foothold in the Toronto club scene through Elvis Mondays, Pezz met many other local bands like The Salads and A Flatulite, expanding their network and securing more gigs. "And from there, we met so many other bands like the salads, a flatulite, just a lot of Toronto bands and we got into different circles and started getting other gigs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Limited Release Demo
podcast.body: Only around 100 copies of the "Demoluca" demo tape were produced, making it a highly sought-after item that occasionally appears on sites like eBay. "There was only a hundred copies made. Well, look at this. From Demoluca, here's Pez, and Happy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pez - Genre Fluidity
podcast.body: In the early Toronto music scene, Pezz did not strictly adhere to one genre. They played with diverse bands, including punk rock/ska bands like Flashlight Brown and various hard rock acts, without feeling the need to fit into a specific scene. "But back in the day, like we would play with, you know, flashlight brown and there were like a punk rock on a scob band. And then we'd play with like hard rock bands and we'd play... Like there was no... It didn't matter, necessarily what Jean-Roy, you were, it's just... You were part of this thing, you know? So every night you can go out and play with all these different kinds of bands."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Recording in Parents' Basement
podcast.body: Pez recorded their first four-song demo, "Demoluca," in 1994 in "Johnny's" parents' basement, utilizing a Tascam 4-track recorder. "There was a couple of tapes we recorded first in my parents' basement on Johnny's. He used to have a four track and back then it was a hard thing to find and he had a task in four tracks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Securing First Toronto Gigs
podcast.body: The band gained their first major opportunity in downtown Toronto by providing their "Demoluca" tape to William New, who organized "Elvis Mondays" at the Old Elmucongo. A last-minute cancellation led to their initial booking, which subsequently led to more gigs and networking with other local bands like The Salads and A Flatulite. "Our first big break downtown was we gave this tape to a guy named William New, who had the oldest Mondays at the Old Elmucongo."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The Billy Talent EP - "Saved the Band"
podcast.body: The 2001 "Billy Talent EP" (often referred to as the green album demo) is credited by the band members as having "saved the band" during a particularly difficult period that included Aaron Solowaniak's MS diagnosis and John Gallant's temporary departure. This EP represented a rebirth for the group. "That's actually a CD that saved the band. But that was a dark time, though, as well, because- Just prior to that, because that was a rebirth, like that CD, that green EP represented- Like the rebirth of our band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Wattouche Production and Promotion
podcast.body: The band self-produced 500 copies of "Wattouche" using Aaron Solowaniak's credit card. They attempted to promote the album by participating in events like Canadian Music Week, and the self-released record garnered reviews despite having no label support. "So then when we finished this record, we, you know, we... Again, on Aaron's credit card, we produced I think 500 or something like that at the first run. ... And then, you know, we would try to get on to like Canadian music week and all those, that kind of circuit. ... It did get out a little bit. Yeah. So we were pretty... You had no management either. No management. Nothing. Yeah, it was a handful of like temporary managers at the time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Wattouche Recording - Tattoo Music Studio
podcast.body: Their 1999 full-length album, "Wattouche," was recorded at Tattoo Music, a studio primarily used for jingles. The band was able to record there for free at night. "So it was a big deal for us and he was working in a place called Tattoo Music. And we would go and record at night when the studio, because it was like a jingle kind of studio, but we would go record there at night for free."
